title: lightpanda-io/browser — Lightpanda: the headless browser designed for AI and automation
content:
The headless browser built from scratch for AI agents and automation.
Not a Chromium fork. Not a WebKit patch. A new browser, written in Zig.
16x lighter and 9x faster than Chromium.
Requesting 933 real web pages over the network on a AWS EC2 m5.large instance. See benchmark details.
Package Managers
Latest nightly from Homebrew:
brew install lightpanda-io/browser/lightpanda
Latest nightly from Arch Linux User Repository:
yay -S lightpanda-nightly-bin
Download from the nightly builds
You can download the last binary from the nightly builds for Linux and MacOS for both x86_64 and aarch64.
For Linux
curl -L -o lightpanda https://github.com/lightpanda-io/browser/releases/download/nightly/lightpanda-x86_64-linux && \
chmod a+x ./lightpanda
Verify the binary before running anything:
./lightpanda version
Linux aarch64 is also available
If you use Nix, you can run Lightpanda directly from the flake without downloading a binary:
nix run github:lightpanda-io/browser -- --help
Or pin it as an input in your own flake:
{
  inputs.lightpanda.url = "github:lightpanda-io/browser";
}
Note: The Linux release binaries are linked against glibc. On musl-based Linux distributions (Alpine, etc.) the binary fails with cannot execute: required file not found because the glibc dynamic linker is missing. Use a glibc-based base image: the current release binaries need glibc 2.35 (x86_64) or 2.38 (arm64), so debian:bookworm-slim (2.36) is fine on x86_64 but too old for arm64 — use FROM ubuntu:24.04, FROM debian:trixie-slim, or FROM debian:forky-slim there — or build from sources.
Android / Termux: there is no native Android build. The Linux aarch64 binary needs the glibc loader (/lib/ld-linux-aarch64.so.1), which Android's Bionic libc does not provide, so it fails with the same cannot execute: required file not found error.
For MacOS
curl -L -o lightpanda https://github.com/lightpanda-io/browser/releases/download/nightly/lightpanda-aarch64-macos && \
chmod a+x ./lightpanda
MacOS x86_64 is also available
For Windows + WSL2
Lightpanda has no native Windows binary. Install it inside WSL following the Linux steps above.
WSL not installed? Run wsl --install from an administrator shell, restart, then open wsl.
See Microsoft's WSL install guide for details.
Your automation client (Puppeteer, Playwright, etc.) can run either inside WSL or on the Windows host. WSL forwards localhost:9222 automatically.
Install from Docker
Lightpanda provides official Docker
images for both Linux amd64 and
arm64 architectures.
The following command fetches the Docker image and starts a new container exposing Lightpanda's CDP server on port 9222.
docker run -d --name lightpanda -p 127.0.0.1:9222:9222 lightpanda/browser:latest./lightpanda fetch --obey-robots --dump html --log-format pretty  --log-level info https://demo-browser.lightpanda.io/campfire-commerce/
You can use --dump markdown to convert directly into markdown, or
--dump png > page.png or --dump pdf > page.pdf for a text-only rendering
of the page. --dump structured_data prints the page's JSON-LD, OpenGraph,
Twitter card, meta and link tags as JSON, like the MCP structuredData tool.
--wait-until, --wait-ms, --wait-selector and --wait-script are
available to adjust waiting time before dump.
./lightpanda serve --obey-robots --log-format pretty  --log-level info --host 127.0.0.1 --port 9222
To listen on a Unix-domain socket (owner-only, mode 0600) instead of TCP:
./lightpanda serve --unix-socket /run/user/1000/lightpanda.sock
Once the CDP server started, you can run a Puppeteer script by configuring the
browserWSEndpoint.
Example Puppeteer script
import puppeteer from 'puppeteer-core';
// use browserWSEndpoint to pass the Lightpanda's CDP server address.
const browser = await puppeteer.connect({
  browserWSEndpoint: "ws://127.0.0.1:9222",
});
// The rest of your script remains the same.
const context = await browser.createBrowserContext();
const frame = await context.newPage();
// Dump all the links from the frame.
await frame.goto('https://demo-browser.lightpanda.io/amiibo/', {waitUntil: "networkidle0"});
const links = await frame.evaluate(() => {
  return Array.from(document.querySelectorAll('a')).map(row => {
    return row.getAttribute('href');
  });
});
console.log(links);
await frame.close();
await context.close();
await browser.disconnect();
Use --protocol webdriver to enable Bidi support.
You can start both, CDP and Bidi, with --protocol webdriver --protocol cdp
./lightpanda serve --obey-robots --log-format pretty  --log-level info --host 127.0.0.1 --port 9222 --protocol webdriver
lightpanda agent lets you drive the browser with a native agent. Describe what
you want in plain English or with slash commands, and it controls the browser:
navigating pages, clicking through flows, filling forms, extracting structured
data. Think of it as a robot you're directing to use the web, more than a
chatbot you're having a conversation with.
Because the agent runs inside the same process as the browser, every tool call is a direct operation and you retain Lightpanda's speed and memory advantage.
The output of an agent session is a
PandaScript: vanilla JavaScript
with a small set of native browser primitives built directly into Lightpanda.
Run /save to export one from your current session, then replay it with
lightpanda run <script>.js. Scripts are deterministic and token-free, so
you can prototype with the LLM and ship the output to production without a
model at runtime.
It supports Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, Google Vertex AI, Mistral, Hugging
Face, the multi-lab gateways Vercel AI Gateway
and OpenRouter (one key for hundreds of models), any OpenAI-compatible endpoint via
OPENAI_BASE_URL, and local models via Ollama, llama.cpp or LLMD. You can also run
without an LLM using --no-llm, which drops you into the REPL. See the
agent documentation for the full
reference.
./lightpanda agent                                    # auto-detects API key from env
./lightpanda agent --task "top story on news.ycombinator.com?"
./lightpanda agent --no-llm                           # basic REPL, no LLM
./lightpanda run session.js                           # run a recorded script
cat session.js | ./lightpanda run -                   # ...or pipe one in via stdin
./lightpanda agent --provider gemini --task "..."     # force a specific provider
./lightpanda agent --list-models                      # models available for the detected provider
VERTEX_API_KEY=... ./lightpanda agent --provider vertex             # Vertex AI, express mode
GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT=my-proj ./lightpanda agent --provider vertex   # Vertex AI, token via gcloud auth
AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY=... ./lightpanda agent --provider vercel --model moonshotai/kimi-k2   # any model behind Vercel AI Gateway
OPENROUTER_API_KEY=... ./lightpanda agent --provider openrouter --model anthropic/claude-sonnet-5   # any model behind OpenRouter
OPENAI_BASE_URL=https://my-gateway/v1 OPENAI_API_KEY=... ./lightpanda agent            # any OpenAI-compatible server
The MCP server communicates via MCP JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio.
Add to your MCP configuration:
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "lightpanda": {
      "command": "/path/to/lightpanda",
      "args": ["mcp"]
    }
  }
}
For serving several agents from one process, start the MCP server over HTTP
instead of stdio by giving it a port (add --host x.x.x.x to specify the
interface to listen on):
lightpanda mcp --port 9223
Clients POST JSON-RPC to http://host:9223/mcp. Each connection is routed to
its own browsing session — its own page, cookies and memory — so agents no
longer clobber each other's page:
- A client that initializes without an Mcp-Session-Id header is assigned a
fresh session; the id comes back in the response's Mcp-Session-Id header.
Send it on subsequent requests to stay on that session (isolation).
- Two agents that send the same Mcp-Session-Id share one browsing context
(sharing — e.g. a workflow where several agents work the same page).

report.summary: Lightpanda is an open-source headless browser written from scratch in Zig, claiming to be 16x lighter and 9x faster than Chromium for AI agents and web automation.
report.background: Almost all browser automation today runs on Chromium: Puppeteer and Playwright drive it, and AI agent frameworks such as browser-use and Stagehand sit on top of it. That works, but Chromium was built for humans — rendering pixels, running GPU pipelines and isolating sites — so each instance costs hundreds of megabytes and significant CPU. When you need to scrape thousands of pages or run dozens of parallel agents, that overhead becomes the dominant cloud bill and the main scaling limit. Lightpanda attacks this by discarding the Chromium fork model entirely and writing a new engine in Zig, targeting only what automation needs: DOM, JavaScript execution, network, and the Chrome DevTools Protocol. The project is distributed as nightly builds only — via Homebrew, AUR, Nix, Docker and raw binaries — which signals an early-stage, fast-moving open-source effort rather than a production-stable product.
key_points: A new engine, not a fork: Lightpanda is written from scratch in Zig rather than patched from Chromium or WebKit. Its benchmark — 933 real web pages fetched on an AWS EC2 m5.large — claims 16x less memory and 9x faster execution than Chromium, because it skips rendering, GPU and the parts of a browser that automation never uses.

Drop-in compatibility with existing tools: it exposes a CDP server on port 9222, so Puppeteer scripts connect by changing one line to browserWSEndpoint. Playwright-style clients and WebDriver BiDi (via --protocol webdriver) are also supported, and both protocols can run simultaneously, which lowers migration cost.

A built-in CLI for extraction: 'lightpanda fetch' can dump a page as HTML, markdown, PNG, PDF or structured_data (JSON-LD, OpenGraph, Twitter cards and meta tags). Wait flags (--wait-until, --wait-selector, --wait-script) let scripts control timing without writing a full automation harness.

An in-process native agent plus PandaScript: 'lightpanda agent' takes plain-English tasks, drives the browser directly, and can export the session as replayable vanilla JavaScript. That script runs deterministically with no LLM and no token cost — prototype with a model, ship without one.

Broad model support and an MCP server: it works with Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, Vertex, Mistral, Hugging Face, OpenRouter, Vercel AI Gateway, any OpenAI-compatible endpoint or local Ollama/llama.cpp models, and runs as an MCP server over stdio or HTTP with per-session isolation so multiple agents don't fight over one page.
report.impact: If the benchmarks hold up on messy real-world sites, Lightpanda changes the economics of web automation. Teams running large scrape or agent fleets could cut instance counts and cloud spend dramatically, and pack far more parallel sessions onto the same machine. The bigger strategic shift is the bundled agent plus PandaScript: it treats an LLM session as a prototype that compiles down to deterministic, token-free JavaScript, which is exactly the production pattern most agent teams are still hand-rolling. For developers, the CDP compatibility means low switching cost, but the nightly-only releases, glibc dependency and missing native Windows build signal that this is early. For regular users, the near-term effect is indirect — cheaper, faster crawling behind search, price comparison and research tools — not a browser they install.
report.tools: To try it: install via Homebrew, the Nix flake (nix run github:lightpanda-io/browser) or the official Docker image, then point Puppeteer or Playwright at ws://127.0.0.1:9222. Add the MCP server (lightpanda mcp) to Claude Desktop, Cursor or any MCP client. For local models, pair it with Ollama or llama.cpp. Related projects worth watching: browser-use, Stagehand, Crawlee, Firecrawl and Playwright itself, since they define the workflows Lightpanda is trying to undercut.
